tools.name: wait
tools.description:
Waits on a yielded `exec` cell and returns new output or completion.
- Use `wait` only after `exec` returns `Script running with cell ID ...`.
- `cell_id` identifies the running `exec` cell to resume.
- `yield_time_ms` controls how long to wait for more output before yielding again. Defaults to 10000 ms.
- `max_tokens` limits how much new output this wait call returns. Defaults to 10000 tokens.
- `terminate: true` stops the running cell; false or omitted waits for output.
- `wait` returns only the new output since the last yield, or the final completion or termination result for that cell.
- If the cell is still running, `wait` may yield again with the same `cell_id`.
- If the cell has already finished, `wait` returns the completed result and closes the cell.

cell_id.description: Identifier of the running exec cell.

max_tokens.description: Output token budget for this wait call. Defaults to 10000 tokens.

terminate.description: True stops the running exec cell; false or omitted waits for output.

yield_time_ms.description: Wait before yielding more output. Defaults to 10000 ms.

tools.name: request_user_input
tools.description: Request user input for one to three short questions and wait for the response. This tool is only available in Plan mode.

questions.description: Questions to show the user. Prefer 1 and do not exceed 3

header.description: Short header label shown in the UI (12 or fewer chars).

options.description: Provide 2-3 mutually exclusive choices. Put the recommended option first and suffix its label with "(Recommended)". Do not include an "Other" option in this list; the client will add a free-form "Other" option automatically.

description.description: One short sentence explaining impact/tradeoff if selected.

question.description: Single-sentence prompt shown to the user.

tools.name: request_user_input_async
tools.description: Ask the user one or more questions during ongoing work. Use this tool only to request missing information, preferences, constraints, clarification, or approval. The tool returns immediately without ending the turn or waiting for a reply; any reply arrives asynchronously as a new user message. Keep questions concise, self-contained, and easy to understand, using a level of detail appropriate to the user and task. The UI always allows a free-text answer, including when suggested options are provided. A preselected option is not submitted automatically.

questions.description: One or more self-contained questions to present together, in display order.

options.description: Suggested answers, in display order. Put the recommended answer first; the first option is preselected by default. The user can select one option or enter a free-text answer. Do not include an Other option or a free-text placeholder; the UI provides free-text input automatically. Omit options for a free-text-only question.

title.description: The complete question shown to the user, including any context needed to answer it.

tools.name: send_message_to_user_async
tools.description: Send a concise message that needs the user's attention during ongoing work. The tool returns immediately without ending the turn or waiting for a reply; any reply arrives asynchronously as a new user message. Use this tool to report a critical blocker or a finding that may change the task's direction, or to answer a user question or status request received while work is still in progress. Use this tool when a message needs the user's immediate attention; use commentary for routine progress and intermediate context. Use clear formatting, such as bolding questions, to make requests easy to notice and answer.

message.description: The concise question or update to send to the user.

tools.name: clock
tools.description: Tools for reading and waiting on time.

tools.name: sleep
tools.description: Pause execution for a specified duration. The sleep ends early when new input arrives for the active turn. Returns the elapsed wall-clock time.

duration_ms.description: How long to sleep in milliseconds. Must be between 1 and 43200000.

tools.name: collaboration
tools.description: Tools for spawning and managing sub-agents.

tools.name: followup_task
tools.description: Send a follow-up task to an existing non-root target agent and trigger a turn if it is idle. If the target is already running, deliver the task promptly at message boundaries while sampling, or after the pending tool call completes.

message.description: Message text to send to the target agent.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to send a follow-up task to (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: interrupt_agent
tools.description: Interrupt an agent's current turn, if any, and return its previous status. The agent remains available for messages and follow-up tasks.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to interrupt (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: list_agents
tools.description: List live agents in the current root thread tree. Optionally filter by task-path prefix.

path_prefix.description: Task-path prefix filter without a trailing slash. Omit to list all live agents.

tools.name: send_message
tools.description: Send a message to an existing agent. The message will be delivered promptly. Does not trigger a new turn.

message.description: Message text to queue on the target agent.

target.description: Relative or canonical task name to message (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: spawn_agent
tools.description:
Available model overrides (optional; inherited parent model is preferred):
- `gpt-6.2-sol`: Fast, go-to model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority, ultrafast.
- `gpt-6.2-astra`: Our most capable model for complex coding and professional work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority, ultrafast.
- `gpt-6.1-terra`: Efficient model that excels at visual understanding and computer use. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6.1-sol`: Previous generation model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority, ultrafast.
- `gpt-6-astra`: Previous generation model for complex coding and professional work. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority, ultrafast.
- `gpt-6-sol`: Legacy model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6-luna`: Fast and affordable model for easier tasks. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.6-sol`: Legacy model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.6-terra`: Legacy balanced model for agentic coding. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.6-luna`: Legacy fast model for simpler tasks. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max. Service tiers: priority.
        Spawns an agent to work on the specified task. If your current task is `/root/task1` and you spawn_agent with task_name "task_3" the agent will have canonical task name `/root/task1/task_3`.
You are then able to refer to this agent as `task_3` or `/root/task1/task_3` interchangeably. However an agent `/root/task2/task_3` would only be able to communicate with this agent via its canonical name `/root/task1/task_3`.
The spawned agent will have the same tools as you and the ability to spawn its own subagents.

It will be able to send you and other running agents messages, and its final answer will be provided to you when it finishes.
The new agent's canonical task name will be provided to it along with the message.

Note that passing `fork_turns="none"` will not pass any surrounding context to the spawned subagent, which may cause the agent to lack the context it needs to complete its task, whereas `fork_turns="all"` will provide the subagent with all surrounding context.

fork_turns.description: Parent history to inherit. Defaults to `all`; use `none` to start without parent history. Only `all` and `none` are supported.

message.description: Initial plain-text task for the new agent.

model.description: Model override for the new agent. Omit unless an explicit override is needed.

reasoning_effort.description: Reasoning effort override for the new agent. Omit to inherit the parent effort.

task_name.description: Task name for the new agent. Use lowercase letters, digits, and underscores.

tools.description: Wait for a mailbox update from any live agent, including queued messages and final-status notifications. The wait also ends early when new user input is steered into the active turn. Does not return the content; returns either a summary of which agents have updates (if any), an interruption summary for steered input, or a timeout summary if no activity arrives before the deadline.

timeout_ms.description: Timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000, min 10000, max 3600000.

## Memory

You have access to a memory folder with guidance from prior runs. It can save
time and help you stay consistent. Use it whenever it is likely to help.

Decision boundary: should you use memory for a new user query?

- Skip memory ONLY when the request is clearly self-contained and does not need
  workspace history, conventions, or prior decisions.
- Hard skip examples: current time/date, simple translation, simple sentence
  rewrite, one-line shell command, trivial formatting.
- Use memory by default when ANY of these are true:
  - the query mentions workspace/repo/module/path/files in MEMORY_SUMMARY below,
  - the user asks for prior context / consistency / previous decisions,
  - the task is ambiguous and could depend on earlier project choices,
  - the ask is a non-trivial and related to MEMORY_SUMMARY below.
- If unsure, do a quick memory pass.

Memory layout (general -> specific):

- C:\Users\lcvle\.codex\memories/memory_summary.md (already provided below; do NOT open again)
- C:\Users\lcvle\.codex\memories/MEMORY.md (searchable registry; primary file to query)
- C:\Users\lcvle\.codex\memories/skills/<skill-name>/ (skill folder)
  - SKILL.md (entrypoint instructions)
  - scripts/ (optional helper scripts)
  - examples/ (optional example outputs)
  - templates/ (optional templates)
- C:\Users\lcvle\.codex\memories/rollout_summaries/ (per-rollout recaps + evidence snippets)
  - The paths of these entries can be found in C:\Users\lcvle\.codex\memories/MEMORY.md or C:\Users\lcvle\.codex\memories/rollout_summaries/ as `rollout_path`
  - These files are append-only `jsonl`: `session_meta.payload.id` identifies the session, `turn_context` marks turn boundaries, `event_msg` is the lightweight status stream, and `response_item` contains actual messages, tool calls, and tool outputs.
  - For efficient lookup, prefer matching the filename suffix or `session_meta.payload.id`; avoid broad full-content scans unless needed.

Quick memory pass (when applicable):

1. Skim the MEMORY_SUMMARY below and extract task-relevant keywords.
2. Search C:\Users\lcvle\.codex\memories/MEMORY.md using those keywords.
3. Only if MEMORY.md directly points to rollout summaries/skills, open the 1-2
   most relevant files under C:\Users\lcvle\.codex\memories/rollout_summaries/ or
   C:\Users\lcvle\.codex\memories/skills/.
4. If above are not clear and you need exact commands, error text, or precise evidence, search over `rollout_path` for more evidence.
5. If there are no relevant hits, stop memory lookup and continue normally.

Quick-pass budget:

- Keep memory lookup lightweight: ideally <= 4-6 search steps before main work.
- Avoid broad scans of all rollout summaries.

During execution: if you hit repeated errors, confusing behavior, or suspect
relevant prior context, redo the quick memory pass.

How to decide whether to verify memory:

- Consider both risk of drift and verification effort.
- If a fact is likely to drift and is cheap to verify, verify it before
  answering.
- If a fact is likely to drift but verification is expensive, slow, or
  disruptive, it is acceptable to answer from memory in an interactive turn,
  but you should say that it is memory-derived, note that it may be stale, and
  consider offering to refresh it live.
- If a fact is lower-drift and expensive to verify, it is usually fine to
  answer from memory directly.

When answering from memory without current verification:

- If you rely on memory for a fact that you did not verify in the current turn,
  say so briefly in the final answer.
- If that fact is plausibly drift-prone or comes from an older note, older
  snapshot, or prior run summary, say that it may be stale or outdated.
- If live verification was skipped and a refresh would be useful in the
  interactive context, consider offering to verify or refresh it live.
- Do not present unverified memory-derived facts as confirmed-current.
- Prefer a short refresh offer for interactive questions, especially about prior
  results, commands, timing, or older snapshots.

Memory citation requirements:

- If ANY relevant memory files were used: append exactly one
`<oai-mem-citation>` block as the VERY LAST content of the final reply.
  Normal responses should include the answer first, then append the
`<oai-mem-citation>` block at the end.
- Use this exact structure for programmatic parsing:
```
<oai-mem-citation>
<citation_entries>
MEMORY.md:234-236|note=[responsesapi citation extraction code pointer]
rollout_summaries/2026-02-17T21-23-02-LN3m-example.md:10-12|note=[weekly report format]
</citation_entries>
<rollout_ids>
019c6e27-e55b-73d1-87d8-4e01f1f75043
019c7714-3b77-74d1-9866-e1f484aae2ab
</rollout_ids>
</oai-mem-citation>
```
- `citation_entries` is for rendering:
  - one citation entry per line
  - format: `<file>:<line_start>-<line_end>|note=[<how memory was used>]`
  - use file paths relative to the memory base path (for example, `MEMORY.md`,
    `rollout_summaries/...`, `skills/...`)
  - only cite files actually used under the memory base path (do not cite
    workspace files as memory citations)
  - if you used `MEMORY.md` and then a rollout summary/skill file, cite both
  - list entries in order of importance (most important first)
  - `note` should be short, single-line, and use simple characters only (avoid
    unusual symbols, no newlines)
- `rollout_ids` is for us to track what previous rollouts you find useful:
  - include one rollout id per line
  - rollout ids should look like UUIDs (for example,
    `019c6e27-e55b-73d1-87d8-4e01f1f75043`)
  - include unique ids only; do not repeat ids
  - an empty `<rollout_ids>` section is allowed if no rollout ids are available
  - you can find rollout ids in rollout summary files and MEMORY.md
  - do not include file paths or notes in this section
  - For every `citation_entries`, try to find and cite the corresponding rollout id if possible
- Never include memory citations inside pull-request messages.
- Never cite blank lines; double-check ranges.

Updating memories:

You can update the memories **only** when explicitly asked by the user. This must always come from a direct request from the user.
- Write your update in C:\Users\lcvle\.codex\memories/extensions/ad_hoc/notes/
- Each update must be one small file containing what you want to add/delete/update from the memories.
- The name of this file must be `<timestamp>-<short slug>.md`
- Do not try to edit the memory files yourself, only add one update note in C:\Users\lcvle\.codex\memories/extensions/ad_hoc/notes/

description: "Enforces strict Windows 11 and PowerShell 7+ (pwsh.exe) execution standards, preventing Bash/Linux hallucinations, interactive hangs, encoding corruption, and file-locking errors. Mandatory default runtime skill: ALWAYS read and apply before writing or executing any shell command, PowerShell script, or terminal pipeline in this Windows 11 + PowerShell 7+ environment."

# Windows 11 & PowerShell 7+ Agent Execution Skill

**Version:** 2.1.0 | **Platform:** Windows 11 (x64/ARM64) | **Shell:** PowerShell 7.4+ (`pwsh.exe`)

You are operating strictly inside a **Windows 11 (x64/ARM64)** environment using **PowerShell 7+ (`pwsh.exe`)**.
**CRITICAL DIRECTIVE:** Do NOT hallucinate Bash, POSIX, WSL, `cmd.exe`, or legacy Windows PowerShell 5.1 (`powershell.exe`) behaviors. Every command, script, and pipeline you generate must be valid, non-interactive, idiomatic PowerShell 7+.

> **Governing Workspace Protocol (`AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md` Precedence):** Where this skill and `AGENTS.md` differ, `AGENTS.md` prevails:
> 1. **`temp\` Isolation (§3):** The system/user default temporary locations are **forbidden**: `C:\Windows\Temp`, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp`, `/tmp`, and the unconfigured default values of `$env:TEMP`, `$env:TMP`, and `$env:TMPDIR`. Do not use `[System.IO.Path]::GetTempPath()` to select a temporary root. Every temporary file, script, log, emulator/AVD, build output, and cache lives in `<repo>\temp\`; when a tool honors those environment variables, set them to paths under `<repo>\temp\` first, then delete task-owned temporary data before completion.
> 2. **Direct PowerShell and Runtime Credentials (§3):** Execute directly in `pwsh.exe`, with the explicit working directory and task-local temporary variables. Do not launch `op run`, `opx.py`, or an `op-terminal` wrapper. Read authorized credentials from the process environment at call time; never print them, persist them, or put them in command-line arguments. Give repository code only the credentials its authorized operation requires. Linear, Composio, GitHub, Slack, Firebase, and Cloudflare use the official APIs specified in the current `AGENTS.md`, never their MCP servers; `gh` remains an allowed GitHub auxiliary channel.
> 3. **Encoding, Line Endings & Lockfiles (§6.B, §6.D):** Preserve existing encodings and line endings (`core.autocrlf=false`) when editing existing files; never hand-edit or regex lockfiles (`package-lock.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `Cargo.lock`). Edit dependency declarations deliberately and regenerate lockfiles with the official tool in the no-code mode required by `AGENTS.md`; do not apply blind regex replacements to manifests or prose.
> 4. **Process Termination Scope (§3):** Terminate only processes spawned by the current task; preserve editors, data, and processes of concurrent tasks. Before recursive deletion or moving, resolve and verify that the absolute target is within the task-owned directory.
> 5. **Repository Sessions and Validation (§3–§4):** Before editing a repository, use a repository/worktree-rooted native agent session with Entire capture. Dependency-version changes are validated by CI, with only the documented Wrangler type-generation exception. Local Cargo/Rust execution is permitted when applicable, with targets and caches inside task-owned `temp\`. Never execute untrusted contributor code locally.

---

## 1. Environment & Shell Fundamentals

### 1.1 Shell Binary & Subshells
- **Primary Binary:** Always invoke `pwsh.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -Command "..."` when spawning subshells or executing inline commands.
- **Forbidden Shells:** Never invoke `powershell.exe` (legacy 5.1), `cmd.exe`, `bash.exe`, or `wsl.exe` unless explicitly requested by the user for a specific cross-environment task.

### 1.2 Path Separators, Wildcard Traps & Resolution
- **Path Construction:** Prefer `Join-Path -Path $base -ChildPath "sub\file.txt"` or standard backslashes (`\`).
- **Quoting Paths:** Always wrap paths in double quotes (`"C:\Program Files\App\bin.exe"`) or single quotes if no variable interpolation is required (`'C:\Path With Spaces\file.txt'`).
- **The Bracket Wildcard Trap (`-LiteralPath` vs `-Path`):**
  - PowerShell treats `[` and `]` as wildcard characters in `-Path`. In modern web frameworks (Next.js, SvelteKit, Nuxt, Astro), routes like `app/users/[id]/page.tsx` will **FAIL** with `-Path`.
  - **Rule:** ALWAYS prefer `-LiteralPath` over `-Path` for `Get-Content`, `Set-Content`, `Test-Path`, `Copy-Item`, `Move-Item`, and `Remove-Item` whenever targeting a specific file or directory path.

### 1.3 Standard Windows Environment Variables
Never use `/tmp`, `/var`, `/etc`, `/usr/bin`, or `~` inside native external calls. Use PowerShell environment variables:
- **Temp Directory:** `<repo>\temp\` inside the repository or worktree where the task runs. Never use the system/user default values of `$env:TEMP`, `$env:TMP`, or `$env:TMPDIR`, and never use `[System.IO.Path]::GetTempPath()` to choose the root; point those variables at a folder under `<repo>\temp\` before invoking tools that read them.
- **User Home:** `$HOME` or `$env:USERPROFILE`
- **AppData (Roaming):** `$env:APPDATA` (`C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming`)
- **AppData (Local):** `$env:LOCALAPPDATA` (`C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local`)
- **Program Files:** `$env:ProgramFiles` and `${env:ProgramFiles(x86)}`
- **ProgramData:** `$env:ProgramData` (`C:\ProgramData`)
- **Path Variable Manipulation:** Windows uses semicolons (`;`), NOT colons (`:`), to separate `PATH` entries:
  ```powershell
  $env:PATH = "C:\my\custom\bin;$env:PATH"
  ```

### 1.4 File Encoding & Line Endings
- **UTF-8 No BOM Standard:** PowerShell 7+ defaults to `utf8NoBOM`, which you must explicitly enforce when writing new files:
  ```powershell
  Set-Content -LiteralPath "file.txt" -Value $content -Encoding utf8NoBOM
  Out-File -LiteralPath "file.txt" -InputObject $content -Encoding utf8NoBOM
  ```
- **Line Endings (CRLF vs LF):** Windows uses `CRLF` (`` `r`n ``) by default. When generating shell scripts (`.sh`), Dockerfiles, or config files for Linux containers, force `LF` (`` `n ``) and use `-NoNewline`:
  ```powershell
  ($lines -join "`n") | Set-Content -LiteralPath "entrypoint.sh" -Encoding utf8NoBOM -NoNewline
  ```
  When editing existing repository files, preserve their current encoding and line endings (`core.autocrlf=false`).

---

## 2. Strict Bash-to-PowerShell 7 Translation Matrix

**NEVER** execute `grep`, `sed`, `awk`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `touch`, `rm -rf`, `cp -r`, `mv`, `export`, `which`, `find`, `chmod`, `chown`, `sudo`, `ps aux`, `kill -9`, `lsof`, `xargs`, or `wc`.

| Bash / Linux Command | Idiomatic PowerShell 7+ Equivalent |
| :--- | :--- |
| `grep -rn "pattern" .` | `rg -n -- "pattern" .` (use `Select-String` if `rg` is unavailable) |
| `grep -i "pattern" file.txt` | `Select-String -LiteralPath "file.txt" -Pattern "pattern"` (case-insensitive by default; use `-CaseSensitive` if needed) |
| `sed -i 's/old/new/g' file.txt` | Inspect the exact text and apply a bounded edit that preserves encoding and line endings; never regex a lockfile or blindly replace prose/manifests. |
| `cat file.txt` | `Get-Content -LiteralPath "file.txt" -Raw` (`-Raw` reads the entire file as a single string, 10x faster) |
| `head -n 20 file.txt` | `Get-Content -LiteralPath "file.txt" -TotalCount 20` |
| `tail -n 20 file.txt` | `Get-Content -LiteralPath "file.txt" -Tail 20` |
| `tail -f file.txt` | `Get-Content -LiteralPath "file.txt" -Tail 20 -Wait` |
| `touch file.txt` | `New-Item -ItemType File -Path "file.txt" -Force \| Out-Null` |
| `mkdir -p a/b/c` | `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path "a\b\c" -Force \| Out-Null` |
| `rm -rf dir/` | After verifying ownership and the resolved absolute target: `Remove-Item -LiteralPath $taskDirectory -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction Stop` |
| `cp -r src/ dest/` | `Copy-Item -LiteralPath "src" -Destination "dest" -Recurse -Force` |
| `mv old.txt new.txt` | `Move-Item -LiteralPath "old.txt" -Destination "new.txt" -Force` |
| `ls -la` | `Get-ChildItem -Force` |
| `find . -name "*.ts"` | `Get-ChildItem -Path . -Filter "*.ts" -Recurse -File` |
| `export VAR="val"` | `$env:VAR = "val"` |
| `VAR="val" npm test` | `try { $env:VAR = "val"; npm test } finally { Remove-Item Env:\VAR -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue }` |
| `unset VAR` | `Remove-Item Env:\VAR -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` |
| `which node` | `(Get-Command node -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).Source` or `where.exe node` |
| `wc -l file.txt` | `(Get-Content -LiteralPath "file.txt").Count` |
| `ln -s target link` | `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path "link" -Target "target" -Force` |
| `> /dev/null 2>&1` | `*> $null` or `\| Out-Null` |
| `chmod +x script.sh` | `git update-index --chmod=+x script.sh` (Windows FS does not use POSIX bits; use Git index if needed for repos) |
| `sha256sum file.zip` | `(Get-FileHash -LiteralPath "file.zip" -Algorithm SHA256).Hash` |
| `mktemp -d` | `$tmp = Join-Path (Join-Path (git rev-parse --show-toplevel) 'temp') ([System.Guid]::NewGuid().ToString()); New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $tmp -Force \| Out-Null` (inside `<repo>\temp\`, §1.3) |

---

## 3. Quoting, Escaping & Multiline Strings (Agent Pitfalls)

### 3.1 Escape Character Rules
- PowerShell uses the **backtick (`` ` ``)** as its escape character, **NOT** the backslash (`\`).
  - Newline: `` `n ``
  - Carriage Return: `` `r ``
  - Tab: `` `t ``
  - Escaped Double Quote inside Double Quotes: `` `" `` (or `""`)
  - Escaped Dollar Sign (prevent variable interpolation): `` `$ ``
- **Never** write `\"` inside a PowerShell double-quoted string unless specifically formatting arguments for a legacy external C-runtime binary.

### 3.2 Here-Strings for Safe File & Payload Generation
When writing source code, JSON payloads, Python scripts, or Markdown files from the CLI, **ALWAYS use Single-Quoted Here-Strings (`@' ... '@`)**. This prevents PowerShell from expanding `$variables`, subexpressions `$()`, or backticks inside the file content:
```powershell
@'
import os
def main():
    print(f"User path is: {os.environ.get('USERPROFILE')}")
'@ | Set-Content -LiteralPath "app.py" -Encoding utf8NoBOM
```
*(Note: The opening `@'` must be at the very end of its line, and the closing `'@` must be at the very beginning of its own line with no leading spaces).*

### 3.3 Calling External Binaries Safely
- **The Call Operator (`&`):** When executing a command stored in a variable or a quoted path with spaces, you MUST prefix it with `&`:
  ```powershell
  & "$env:ProgramFiles\Git\bin\git.exe" status
  ```
- **Stop-Parsing Token (`--%`):** When calling legacy Windows utilities (`icacls.exe`, `reg.exe`, `sc.exe`, `schtasks.exe`) with arguments containing `{}` or `$`, insert `--%` so PowerShell passes the raw string untouched:
  ```powershell
  icacls.exe --% "C:\MyFolder" /grant Users:(OI)(CI)F
  ```

---

## 4. Modern PowerShell 7+ Syntax & Performance Patterns

- **Pipeline Chain Operators:** Use `&&` (execute if previous succeeded) and `||` (execute if previous failed) just like modern shells:
  ```powershell
  git diff --check && git status --short
  ```
- **Ternary Operator:**
  ```powershell
  $mode = ($env:NODE_ENV -eq 'production') ? 'prod' : 'dev'
  ```
- **Null-Coalescing & Null-Conditional Operators:**
  ```powershell
  $port = $env:PORT ?? 8080
  $cacheDir ??= Join-Path $repoRoot "temp\app-cache"
  $userName = ${response}?.data?.user?.name
  ```
  *(Important: Notice the curly braces `${response}` required when using `?.` null-conditional member access).*
- **Parallel Processing (`ForEach-Object -Parallel`):**
  For heavy I/O or multi-file tasks, use `-Parallel` and pass outer scope variables with `$using:`:
  ```powershell
  $logFiles | ForEach-Object -Parallel {
      Select-String -LiteralPath $_ -Pattern $using:searchPattern
  } -ThrottleLimit 8
  ```
- **Array Append Performance Trap:**
  - **NEVER** do `$arr += $item` inside a loop (PowerShell arrays are immutable; `+=` reallocates and copies the entire array on every iteration).
  - **DO** assign the loop output directly or use a Generic List:
    ```powershell
    $results = foreach ($item in $collection) {
        [PSCustomObject]@{ Name = $item.Name; Processed = $true }
    }
    ```

---

## 5. Error Handling & Native Executable Exit Codes (PS 7.4+ Standard)

### 5.1 Mandatory Fail-Fast Script Header
Start every multi-line command block or `.ps1` script with:
```powershell
$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
$PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference = $true
```
- **Why `$PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference = $true` is critical:** By default in PowerShell, if an external binary (`git`, `npm`, `dotnet`, `cargo`, `pytest`, `tsc`) fails with exit code `1`, PowerShell **continues executing the next line** and ignores `try/catch`! Enabling this variable forces native command non-zero exit codes to throw terminating errors that `try/catch` can catch.

### 5.2 Structured Try/Catch/Finally & Exit Codes
```powershell
try {
    $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
    $PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference = $true

    & npm run build
} catch {
    Write-Error "Execution failed; inspect the task-owned, secret-free diagnostic evidence."
    exit 1
} finally {
    # Cleanup temporary state here
}
```
- Check `$LASTEXITCODE` (integer exit code of the last native binary) or `$?` (boolean success of the last statement) when manual inspection is needed.

### 5.3 Safe Stderr Capture
When capturing combined `stdout` and `stderr` from a native tool (like `git` or `docker` which write informational messages to `stderr`), wrap the invocation so `stderr` does not immediately abort before you inspect `$LASTEXITCODE`:
```powershell
$PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference = $false
$output = & git status --porcelain 2>&1 | ForEach-Object { "$_" }
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) {
    throw "Git failed ($LASTEXITCODE): $($output -join "`n")"
}
$PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference = $true
```

---

## 6. Windows 11 Networking, Ports & Process Management

**Scope of every termination in this skill:** only processes spawned by the current task (`AGENTS.md` §3). Never terminate processes belonging to the operator's editors or concurrent tasks; report concrete conflicts instead.

### 6.1 Inspecting & Freeing Locked Network Ports
- **Find which process is listening on a port (replaces `lsof -i :3000`):**
  ```powershell
  Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 3000 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object LocalAddress, LocalPort, State, OwningProcess,
      @{Name="ProcessName";Expression={(Get-Process -Id $_.OwningProcess -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).ProcessName}},
      @{Name="Path";Expression={(Get-Process -Id $_.OwningProcess -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).Path}}
  ```
- **Kill the process occupying a specific port (only after confirming it belongs to this task):**
  ```powershell
  Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 3000 -State Listen -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object -ExpandProperty OwningProcess -Unique |
    ForEach-Object { Stop-Process -Id $_ -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue }
  ```

### 6.2 Process Management & Zombie Process Trees
- **List process identity and resource usage (replaces `ps aux`):**
  ```powershell
  Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name = 'node.exe'" |
    Select-Object ProcessId, ParentProcessId, Name, WorkingSetSize
  ```
- **Kill an Entire Process Tree (Critical for Node/Python/Java dev servers):**
  `Stop-Process` only kills the parent PID and often leaves child worker processes (`node.exe`, `esbuild.exe`, `uvicorn`) running and locking ports or files. Use `taskkill.exe /F /T` to terminate the entire tree:
  ```powershell
  taskkill.exe /F /T /PID $processId
  ```
- **Run Background / Detached Processes Without Hanging the Agent:**
  Never run `npm run dev &` (in PS, `&` at the end of a line runs a background job that still ties to the session or causes syntax errors in older versions). Use `Start-Process`:
  ```powershell
  $proc = Start-Process -FilePath "pwsh.exe" -ArgumentList "-NoProfile -Command npm run dev" -WorkingDirectory $PWD -WindowStyle Hidden -PassThru
  Write-Output "Started background server with PID: $($proc.Id)"
  ```

### 6.3 Network Diagnostics & HTTP Requests
- **Disable Progress Bars First:** PowerShell's visual progress bar slows `Invoke-WebRequest` and `Expand-Archive` down by up to 10x. Always precede them with:
  ```powershell
  $ProgressPreference = 'SilentlyContinue'
  ```
- **HTTP Requests:**
  - Use `Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "https://api.example.com/data" -Method Get -TimeoutSec 30` for JSON APIs (automatically parses response into PowerShell objects).
  - Use `Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $url -OutFile $dest` for file downloads.
  - If using `curl`, always write `curl.exe` explicitly with the `.exe` extension.
- **Connectivity & DNS Checks:**
  - Port check (replaces `nc -zv`): `Test-NetConnection -ComputerName "127.0.0.1" -Port 5432 -InformationLevel Quiet`
  - DNS resolution (replaces `dig`/`nslookup`): `Resolve-DnsName -Name "example.com" -Type A`

---

## 7. Windows 11 Specifics: File Locks, Registry & Package Management

### 7.1 Handling File Locks (`EPERM` / `EBUSY` / `Access Denied`) & Reparse Points
- Windows strictly locks files opened by running processes. If removing `node_modules`, `.next`, `dist`, `target`, or `.venv` fails with `Access to the path is denied` or `The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process`:
  1. Check for running `node`, `python`, `dotnet`, or `rust-analyzer` processes originating from the current repository directory using `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process`.
  2. Terminate those task-owned processes via `taskkill.exe /F /T /PID <id>` (within the scope of Section 6).
  3. Retry the deletion.
- **Fast Deletion of Massive Directory Trees (`node_modules`):**
  `Remove-Item -Recurse` iterates file-by-file in PowerShell and is slow on 50,000+ files. Use `.NET` directory deletion:
  ```powershell
  if (Test-Path -LiteralPath "node_modules") {
      [System.IO.Directory]::Delete((Resolve-Path -LiteralPath "node_modules").Path, $true)
  }
  ```
- **Junction & Hardlink Check:** Before running `Copy-Item` or `Remove-Item` over customization or workspace directories, inspect `(Get-Item -LiteralPath $target -Force).LinkType` (`Junction`, `SymbolicLink`, `HardLink`) so junctions are not copied onto themselves and shared NTFS hardlinks are not broken unintentionally.

### 7.2 Non-Interactive Package Management
Always pass non-interactive flags so the agent never hangs on a CLI prompt:
- **Winget (Windows Package Manager):**
  ```powershell
  winget install --id Git.Git --exact --source winget --silent --accept-package-agreements --accept-source-agreements --disable-interactivity
  ```
- **Scoop (if installed):** `scoop install jq`
- **Chocolatey (if installed & elevated):** `choco install jq -y --no-progress`

### 7.3 Windows Registry, Services & Elevation
- **Elevation / Administrator Check:**
  Never run `sudo` blindly, and never trigger interactive UAC prompts (`Start-Process -Verb RunAs`, `runas.exe`) from an agent session. Always check if the current `pwsh.exe` session is elevated first:
  ```powershell
  $isAdmin = ([Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal][Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()).IsInRole([Security.Principal.WindowsBuiltInRole]::Administrator)
  if (-not $isAdmin) {
      Write-Error "Administrator privileges required for this operation. Please run the terminal as Administrator."
      exit 1
  }
  ```
- **Registry Operations:**
  Use native PowerShell Registry drives (`HKCU:\` and `HKLM:\`):
  ```powershell
  Get-ItemProperty -Path "HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Themes\Personalize" -Name "AppsUseLightTheme"
  ```
- **Windows Services:**
  Use `Get-Service`, `Start-Service`, `Stop-Service`, and `Restart-Service` instead of `systemctl` or `service`.
- **Clipboard:**
  Use `Get-Clipboard` and `Set-Clipboard` instead of `pbcopy`/`xclip`.

---

## 8. Structured Data & JSON Manipulation Rules

- **Object Pipeline First:** PowerShell commands return rich `.NET` objects, not raw text. Filter with `Where-Object`, project with `Select-Object`, sort with `Sort-Object`, and measure with `Measure-Object`. Never parse PowerShell cmdlet output with `awk`/`sed`/regex when object properties exist!
- **The `ConvertTo-Json` Depth Trap (CRITICAL):**
  `ConvertTo-Json` defaults to `-Depth 2`. Any nested object deeper than 2 levels is silently replaced with its `.NET` type name string (e.g., `"System.Collections.Hashtable"`), corrupting config files!
  - **Rule:** ALWAYS pass `-Depth 10` (or higher, up to `100`) whenever calling `ConvertTo-Json`:
    ```powershell
    $jsonString = $dataObject | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20
    $jsonString | Set-Content -LiteralPath "package.json" -Encoding utf8NoBOM
    ```
- **Safe JSON Parsing:**
  Use `-Raw` with `Get-Content` and `-AsHashtable` with `ConvertFrom-Json` when modifying arbitrary JSON files (such as `tsconfig.json` or `settings.json` which may have keys with hyphens or special characters):
  ```powershell
  $config = Get-Content -LiteralPath "settings.json" -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json -AsHashtable
  $config["editor.formatOnSave"] = $true
  $config | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20 | Set-Content -LiteralPath "settings.json" -Encoding utf8NoBOM
  ```

## List workflow runs for a repository

Lists all workflow runs for a repository. You can use parameters to narrow the list of results. For more information about using parameters, see Parameters.

Anyone with read access to the repository can use this endpoint.

OAuth app tokens and personal access tokens (classic) need the `repo` scope to use this endpoint with a private repository.

This endpoint will return up to 1,000 results for each search when using the following parameters: `actor`, `branch`, `check_suite_id`, `created`, `event`, `head_sha`, `status`.

### Fine-grained access tokens for "List workflow runs for a repository"

This endpoint works with the following fine-grained token types:

  * GitHub App user access tokens
  * GitHub App installation access tokens
  * Fine-grained personal access tokens

The fine-grained token must have the following permission set:

  * "Actions" repository permissions (read)

This endpoint can be used without authentication or the aforementioned permissions if only public resources are requested.

Headers
`accept` string Setting to `application/vnd.github+json` is recommended.

# Configuring default setup for code scanning

Quickly set up code scanning to find and fix vulnerable code automatically.

## Who can use this feature?

Repository owners, organization owners, security managers, and users with the admin role

Code scanning is available for the following repository types:

  * Public repositories on GitHub.com
  * Organization-owned repositories on GitHub Team, GitHub Enterprise Cloud, or GitHub Enterprise Server, with GitHub Code Security enabled.

We recommend that you start using code scanning with default setup. After you've initially configured default setup, you can evaluate code scanning to see how it's working for you and customize it to better meet your needs. For more information, see About setup types for code scanning.

## Prerequisites

Your repository is eligible for default setup for code scanning if:

  * GitHub Actions is enabled.
  * It is publicly visible, or GitHub Code Security is enabled.

Note

If the analyses fail for all CodeQL-supported languages in a repository, default setup will still be enabled, but it will not run any scans or use any GitHub Actions minutes until another CodeQL-supported language is added to the repository or default setup is manually reconfigured, and the analysis of a CodeQL-supported language succeeds.

  1. On GitHub, navigate to the main page of the repository.

Note

If you are configuring default setup on a fork, you must first enable GitHub Actions. To enable GitHub Actions, under your repository name, click Actions, then click I understand my workflows, go ahead and enable them. Be aware that this will enable all existing workflows on your fork.

  2. Under your repository name, click Settings. If you cannot see the "Settings" tab, select the dropdown menu, then click Settings.

Image: Screenshot of a repository header showing the tabs. The "Settings" tab is highlighted by a dark orange outline.

  3. In the "Security and quality" section of the sidebar, click Advanced Security.

  4. Under "Code Security", to the right of "CodeQL analysis", select Set up , then click Default.

Image: Screenshot of the "Code scanning" section of "Advanced Security" settings. The "Default setup" button is highlighted with an orange outline.

You will then see a "CodeQL default configuration" dialog summarizing the code scanning configuration automatically created by default setup.

  5. Optionally, to customize your code scanning setup, click Edit.

     * To add or remove a language from the analysis performed by default setup, select or deselect that language in the "Languages" section.
     * To specify the CodeQL query suite you would like to use, select your preferred query suite in the "Query suites" section.
  6. Review the settings for default setup on your repository, then click Enable CodeQL. This will trigger a workflow that tests the new, automatically generated configuration.

Note

If you are switching to default setup from advanced setup, you will see a warning informing you that default setup will override existing code scanning configurations. This warning means default setup will disable the existing workflow file and block any CodeQL analysis API uploads.

  7. If projects in your repository depend on dependencies in private package registries, you can grant code scanning access to them. This can improve the outcomes and quality of analyses. See Giving security features access to private registries.

  8. Optionally, adjust other configuration options which affect default setup. See Repository properties for code scanning.

  9. Optionally, to view your default setup configuration after enablement, select , then click View CodeQL configuration.

Note

If no pushes and pull requests have occurred in a repository with default setup enabled for 6 months, the weekly schedule will be disabled to save your GitHub Actions minutes. Organization owners can enable monthly scans of inactive repositories. For more information, see Configuring global security settings for your organization.

If your code scanning results are different than you expected, you can check which configurations are active.

If your code scanning results are different than you expected, you may have both default and advanced setup configured for your repository. When you enable default setup, this disables the existing CodeQL workflow file and blocks any CodeQL API analysis from uploading results.

In the "Code scanning" section of the page, next to "CodeQL analysis", click . If there is a Switch to advanced option, you are currently using default setup.

L562: ## gh variable set

# About setup types for code scanning

Depending on your needs, GitHub offers a default or advanced setup for code scanning.

## About default setup

Default setup for code scanning is the quickest, easiest, most low-maintenance way to enable code scanning for your repository. Based on the code in your repository, default setup will automatically create a custom code scanning configuration. You can also customize this configuration, including at scale across your organization, without creating or maintaining a workflow file. See Customization of default setup.

With default setup, the code written in CodeQL-supported languages in your repository will be scanned using CodeQL:

  * When you enable it.
  * On each push to the repository's default branch, or any protected branch. For more information on protected branches, see About protected branches.
  * When creating or committing to a pull request based against the repository's default branch, or any protected branch, excluding pull requests from forks.
  * On a weekly schedule, if a push or pull request has triggered a scan in the last 180 days.
  * Every 30 days for inactive repositories, when enabled by an organization owner. See Configuring global security settings for your organization.

Weekly scheduled scans start only after a push or pull request triggers a scan with default setup enabled. The initial scan and scans triggered by configuration or language changes do not start or extend the weekly schedule. Pushes and pull requests from before default setup was enabled do not count.

### Supported languages

We recommend enabling default setup for eligible repositories if there is any chance the repositories will include at least one CodeQL-supported language in the future. If you enable default setup on a repository that does not include any CodeQL-supported languages, default setup will not run any scans or use any GitHub Actions minutes. If CodeQL-supported languages are added to the repository's default branch, default setup will automatically begin scanning CodeQL-supported languages and using GitHub Actions minutes. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Configuring advanced setup for code scanning

You can configure advanced setup for a repository to find security vulnerabilities in your code using a highly customizable code scanning configuration.

## Who can use this feature?

Repository owners, organization owners, security managers, and users with the admin role

Code scanning is available for the following repository types:

  * Public repositories on GitHub.com
  * Organization-owned repositories on GitHub Team, GitHub Enterprise Cloud, or GitHub Enterprise Server, with GitHub Code Security enabled.

If you do not need a highly customizable code scanning configuration, consider using default setup for code scanning. For more information, see About setup types for code scanning.

## Prerequisites

Your repository is eligible for advanced setup if it meets these requirements.

  * It uses CodeQL-supported languages or you plan to generate code scanning results with a third-party tool.
  * GitHub Actions is enabled.
  * It is publicly visible, or GitHub Code Security is enabled.
See Workflows and Workflow configuration options for code scanning.

Using actions to run code scanning will use minutes. For more information, see GitHub Actions billing.

Note

You can configure code scanning for any public repository where you have write access.

  1. On GitHub, navigate to the main page of the repository.

  2. Under your repository name, click Settings. If you cannot see the "Settings" tab, select the dropdown menu, then click Settings.

Image: Screenshot of a repository header showing the tabs. The "Settings" tab is highlighted by a dark orange outline.

  3. In the "Security and quality" section of the sidebar, click Advanced Security.

  4. In the "CodeQL analysis" row, select Set up , then click Advanced.

Note

If you are switching from default setup to advanced setup, in the "CodeQL analysis" row, select , then click Switch to advanced. In the pop-up window that appears, click Disable CodeQL.

  5. To customize how code scanning scans your code, edit the workflow.

Generally, you can commit the CodeQL analysis workflow without making any changes to it. However, many of the third-party workflows require additional configuration, so read the comments in the workflow before committing.

For more information, see Workflow configuration options for code scanning and CodeQL code scanning for compiled languages.

  6. Click Commit changes... to display the commit changes form.

Image: Screenshot of the form to create a new file. To the right of the file name, a green button, labeled "Commit changes...", is outlined in dark orange.

  7. In the commit message field, type a commit message.

  8. Choose whether you'd like to commit directly to the default branch, or create a new branch and start a pull request.

  9. Click Commit new file to commit the workflow file to the default branch or click Propose new file to commit the file to a new branch.

  10. If you created a new branch, click Create pull request and open a pull request to merge your change into the default branch.

In the suggested CodeQL analysis workflow, code scanning is configured to analyze your code each time you either push a change to the default branch or any protected branches, or raise a pull request against the default branch. As a result, code scanning will now commence.

The `on:pull_request` and `on:push` triggers for code scanning are each useful for different purposes. See Workflow configuration options for code scanning and Triggering a workflow.

For information on bulk enablement, see Configuring advanced setup for code scanning with CodeQL at scale.

## About default setup

Default setup for code scanning is the quickest, easiest, most low-maintenance way to enable code scanning for your repository. Based on the code in your repository, default setup will automatically create a custom code scanning configuration. You can also customize this configuration, including at scale across your organization, without creating or maintaining a workflow file. See Customization of default setup. After enabling default setup, the code written in CodeQL-supported languages in your repository will be scanned using CodeQL:

As massive amounts of AI-generated code are created, developers, teams and agents themselves struggle to link the intent back to the code change itself. Entire captures that missing context and connects it to your Git history. You can use it to:
L92:   * review agent work before merging
L93:   * trace code back to the prompt and session that created it
L94:   * understand why an earlier team or agent chose a particular approach
L95:   * resume or hand off work with its context intact
L96:   * search prior work instead of understanding it from scratch
L97: Taken together, Entire represents one API for your code and the context that created it. A new system of record for agentic coding.
L98: ## How It Works
L99: 
L100:   1. Install the Entire CLI in your repository.
L101:   2. Connect Entire to the coding agent you use.
L102:   3. 【11†Host your repository directly on Entire】 or 【12†mirror an existing GitHub repository】 in the region closest to your agents, and point your Git remote at it.
L103:   4. Entire captures sessions and checkpoints as the agent works, and agents clone and push through your Entire remote.
L104:   5. Continue coding with your agent, enabling it with faster clones and the history behind your work.

L235: # Entire CLI
L236: 
L237: 【117†Entire†entire.com】 is a Git forge built for agent–human collaboration. This CLI is how you and your agents use Entire from the terminal — anything you do on entire.com, you can do here:
L238:   * Distributed Git hosting — host repositories on Entire's Git-compatible server, or mirror your GitHub ones, and replicate them in regions around the world for data residency and the scale of agent traffic. → 【118†Repositories & Git Hosting】
L239:   * Trails — instead of reviewing a diff, get a heads-up display for every change, with customizable evals that agents score on every push. → 【119†Trails】
L240:   * Continuous memory — capture every agent session as a checkpoint linked to your commits; 【120†entire-brain†docs.entire.com】 combines them with 【121†entire-graph†docs.entire.com】's code map into project memory. → 【122†Agent Sessions】
L241: Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot CLI, OpenCode, Antigravity, Factory AI Droid, Pi, and 【123†more†docs.entire.com】, and extends through 【124†plugins】. Pushes through a GitHub mirror still trigger your GitHub Actions, and Trails can also show CI results from Buildkite and Depot.

L25: Copy page Copy page
L26: 
L27: The Codex integration uses Codex’s project-level hook system. Follow 【9†Set Up an Agent】 for shared installation, verification, and troubleshooting steps.
L28: ## Add Codex
L29: 
L30:     `entire agent add codex
L31:     codex
L32:     `
L33: 
L34: Entire writes `.codex/hooks.json`. Codex enables hooks by default beginning with version 0.124.0, so Entire does not create `.codex/config.toml` or set `codex_hooks = true`. The hooks capture session boundaries, prompts, completed turns, file-changing tool calls, and subagent events. Entire reads the full conversation and token usage from Codex rollout files under `~/.codex/` or `CODEX_HOME`.
L35: ## Limitations
L36: 
L37: Ephemeral Codex runs may not provide a transcript path. Entire can process their hook events, but it cannot attach a full transcript without the rollout file. Entire records the subagents that changed files, materializes their transcripts into the parent’s next checkpoint, and attributes their files to the parent session. It skips a subagent that wrote nothing, and it does not yet roll subagent tokens up into the parent session’s totals.
L38: ## Resume and Import
L39: 
L40: `entire session resume BRANCH` restores the recorded session data when needed and prints:
L41: 
L42:     `codex resume SESSION_ID
L43:     `
L44: 
L45: Entire can import existing Codex transcripts from the previous 30 days as read-only checkpoints. See the 【10†`session resume` command reference】 for flags and additional behavior.

L21: # Security & Privacy
L22: 
L23: Where your data lives, which redaction layers run before each write, when data leaves your machine, and how to report security issues
L24: 
L25: Copy page Copy page
L26: 
L27: Entire writes AI session transcripts and checkpoint metadata into your own Git repository, and redacts them before each write. This page covers the trust boundaries, every location Entire writes to or transmits, and which redaction layers cover each one.
L28: We verified the behavior on this page against Entire CLI 0.10.2, except for secret scanner selection, which first appears in `v0.10.3-nightly.202608210613.680d64782`. Run `entire version` to check what you have installed. To configure any of it, see 【9†Privacy and Redaction】 and 【10†Session Storage】; this page describes behavior, those pages hold the settings keys.
L29: ## Where Your Data Lives
L30: 
L31: Checkpoints live in your Git repository. When you push that repository to an `entire://` remote, whether a repository hosted on Entire or a mirror, Entire stores the checkpoints with your code and indexes them for search. Which Git objects hold them depends on the storage backend.
L32: Location  | Holds  | Scope
L33: --- | --- | ---
L34: `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>`  | One ref per checkpoint, carrying that checkpoint’s redacted metadata and transcripts. The default for repositories enabled with CLI 0.10.0 or later  | Local until you push
L35: `entire/checkpoints/v1`  | A single branch carrying every checkpoint, used by repositories enabled before CLI 0.10.0 and by anyone who passes `--checkpoint-backend branch`  | Local until you push
L36: `entire/<commit>-<worktree>`  | Shadow branches: working storage during a live session, including raw, unredacted snapshots of your working tree  | Local. Entire does not push these
L37: `.entire/`  | Settings, redaction rule packs, diagnostic logs, and local runtime state  | Local. Most of it is gitignored
L38: Your own commits  | An `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer naming the checkpoint ID  | Public once you push
L39: Both backends store checkpoint data in the same repository as your code unless you configure a 【11†separate checkpoint repository】. To see or change which backend a repository uses, read `checkpoints.primary.type` in `.entire/settings.json` or pass `--checkpoint-backend` to 【12†`entire configure`】. Anyone with access to your repository can read the checkpoints in it. If your repository is public, so are they.
L40: 【13†`entire checkpoint delete`】 removes a checkpoint locally and from its remotes, but other checkpoints from the same session still carry the full transcript.
L41: Treat redaction as a safety net rather than a guarantee. For customer data, internal credentials, or regulated material, use a private repository.
L42: ## Reporting a Vulnerability
L43: 
L44: Please do not open a public GitHub issue for a security vulnerability.
L45: ## Email security@entire.io
L46: 
L47: Report security vulnerabilities directly. We acknowledge within 48 hours and aim to resolve criticals within 90 days. Full disclosure policy below.
L48: 
L49: Threat Model and Boundaries
L50: Entire is a local development tool that writes to your repository. The protections here assume an attacker who reads your repository, not one who already controls your machine.What redaction is for. It reduces the chance that a credential or a piece of personal data that entered an agent conversation gets committed and pushed. It runs on transcript and metadata content before Entire writes it to a Git object.What redaction does not do:
L51:   * It does not protect a repository from the people who can read it. Anyone with read access reads every checkpoint in it.
L52:   * It does not scan your source code. Redaction covers what Entire writes, not what you commit. A hardcoded secret in a tracked file reaches the remote through your own commit.
L53:   * It does not defend against a compromised machine. An attacker running code as you can read the raw agent transcripts, your Git credentials, and everything under `.entire/` before redaction runs.
L54:   * It does not catch every secret. Detection is pattern- and entropy-based. See Limitations of Redaction below.
L55: Who can read what:
L56: Party  | Reads  | Through
L57: --- | --- | ---
L58: Anyone with read access to your repository  | Redacted checkpoints, your code, and commit trailers  | Normal Git access
L59: Anyone with read access to the checkpoint repository  | Redacted checkpoints only, when you configure a separate 【11†checkpoint remote】  | Normal Git access
L60: entire.com  | The repositories you authorize, and the checkpoints in them  | The 【14†Entire GitHub App】 for GitHub repositories, and Entire’s own Git servers for repositories on Entire. Both read the same redacted content anyone else with repository access reads
L61: Your summary provider  | The compacted transcript for one checkpoint, redacted first, and only when you run `entire checkpoint explain --generate`  | An outbound call to the configured provider
L62: PostHog  | Command names, flag names, and a hashed machine ID, unless you opt out  | Anonymous CLI analytics
L63: Checkpoints travel to the Git remotes you push to. When a remote is on Entire, that includes Entire’s servers, which receive the redacted checkpoints.
L64: 
L65: Data Storage Details
L66: Checkpoint storage holds metadata, not source code. A checkpoint carries `prompt.txt`, `full.jsonl`, `transcript.jsonl`, `metadata.json`, `checkpoint.json`, and an optional `assets/` subtree. Metadata records the paths a session touched, in `files_touched`, and not their contents.Shadow branches hold unredacted source. Shadow branches are the one place Entire writes your source files rather than metadata.
L67: Metadata written to a shadow branch goes through the same redaction pipeline as a committed checkpoint, but code-file snapshots are raw blobs of your working tree, so a hardcoded secret in a tracked file appears in them verbatim. Gitignored files such as `.env` are filtered out of those snapshots as a partial defense. Entire does not push shadow branches and deletes them after a successful push once the session ends cleanly. Do not push one manually.Two redaction passes for metadata.
L68: Entire redacts metadata on the shadow-branch write and again at condensation time, when the session rolls into checkpoint storage. The metadata that lands in checkpoint storage, local or pushed, has been through redaction.`RedactedBytes` type guarantee. The redact package returns a typed wrapper, and the checkpoint stores accept only that type. A code path that tried to write unredacted transcript bytes would fail to compile rather than fail at runtime.Commit trailers.
L69: Entire adds one trailer to your own commits:
L70: 
L71:     `Entire-Checkpoint: 01J9ZQ8F7K3M2N5P6R8T9V0W1X
L72:     `
L73: The value is a checkpoint ID, either a 12-character hex string or a 26-character ULID. It carries no prompt content and no file content. A ULID encodes the millisecond Entire created the checkpoint, so the trailer discloses commit timing to anyone who can read the commit message. The trailer stays in your history after you push, and you can delete the line before committing if you do not want the commit linked.Remote URL redaction in logs.
L74: When a fetch or push fails, error messages and `.entire/logs/` entries strip passwords from URLs, for example `https://user:****@github.com`, so credentials stay out of local log files.
L75: What Redaction Covers
L76: 
L77: Redaction covers the content Entire writes into checkpoint storage. It does not cover everything Entire touches.
L78: Content  | Written to  | Redaction applied  | Reaches a remote
L79: --- | --- | --- | ---
L80: Prompts and transcripts (`prompt.txt`, `full.jsonl`, `transcript.jsonl`)  | Checkpoint storage  | Layers 1 through 8, plus the OpenAI Privacy Filter at push time on the branch backend  | Yes, on push
L81: Checkpoint metadata (`metadata.json`, `checkpoint.json`)  | Checkpoint storage  | Layers 1 through 8. The structural-field skip rules exempt file paths and ID fields, so `files_touched` paths are stored as written  | Yes, on push
L82: Externalized image assets (`assets/`)  | Checkpoint storage  | None. Every layer skips the assets subtree  | Yes, on push, when `redaction.externalize_images` is on
L83: Inline base64 images left in a transcript  | Checkpoint storage  | None. The JSONL skip rules exclude objects whose `type` starts with `image` or equals `base64`  | Yes, on push
L84: Source-file snapshots  | Shadow branch  | None. Raw working-tree blobs, minus gitignored paths  | No, unless you push the shadow branch yourself
L85: Raw agent session files, for example `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/*.jsonl`  | Your agent’s own directory  | None. Entire reads these files and does not rewrite them, because the agent is writing to them concurrently  | No
L86: Diagnostic logs (`.entire/logs/entire.log`)  | Local, gitignored  | Not redacted, but the CLI logs metadata only (IDs, ref names, counts, and timings) and strips passwords from remote URLs  | No
L87: `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer  | Your own commits  | Not applicable. The value is an ID  | Yes, on push
L88: Redaction Layers
L89: 
L90: Nine layers run in this order. Layers 1 through 8 use regexes, entropy scoring, or structural validation during condensation. Layer 9 calls a local model at push time.
L91: 
L92: CLI 0.10.2 uses Betterleaks for layer 2. Scanner selection first appears in `v0.10.3-nightly.202608210613.680d64782`.
L93: #  | Layer  | Runs  | Replacement
L94: --- | --- | --- | ---
L216: Best-effort behavior. Signing does not block a commit. If the signer is unavailable, fails, or waits on a hardware token touch you did not give, Entire creates the commit unsigned and logs a warning to `.entire/logs/`. This keeps CI runs and automated checkpoint saves from losing data.To opt out, see 【27†Checkpoint commit signing】. Opting out does not change how your own commits are signed.
L217: Telemetry and Analytics
L218: 
L219: Once you opt in, the CLI sends anonymous usage analytics to PostHog at `eu.i.posthog.com`, under the event name `cli_command_executed`.What’s captured per command:
L220:   * Command name, for example `entire enable` or `entire checkpoint explain`
L221:   * Selected agent name, or `auto`
L222:   * Whether Entire is enabled in the current repository
L223:   * CLI version
L224:   * OS and architecture, for example `darwin/arm64`
L225:   * Installed Git version, when it can be determined
L226:   * Names of flags passed, not their values
L227: What’s not captured: flag values, prompt text, transcripts, file paths, repository identifiers, GitHub usernames, source code, and IP-derived location. The PostHog client sets `DisableGeoIP: true`.DistinctID is a hashed machine identifier derived from `machineid.ProtectedID`: stable per machine, not directly mappable to a person.Opt out (any one of):
L228:   * Pass `--telemetry=false` on commands that accept it.
L229:   * Set `"telemetry": false` in `.entire/settings.json` or `.entire/settings.local.json`.
L230:   * Set the env var `ENTIRE_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT=1`.
L231: The first run of `entire enable` or `entire configure` asks for telemetry consent interactively, with Yes as the default answer, and `--yes` accepts it. Declining sets the setting to `false`. While the setting is unset, nothing is sent.
L232: 
L233: Recommendations
L234:   * Use a private repository for sensitive work. This is the shortest path to containment, and it does not depend on redaction catching anything.
L235:   * Keep sensitive files out of agent context. Content that never enters a transcript cannot leak through one.
L236:   * Read your checkpoints before the first push. Run 【28†`entire checkpoint explain`】, or inspect the refs directly, the same review you would give any branch about to go public.
L237:   * Enable PII redaction when your agents see customer data. It is off by default.
L238:   * Check whether OPF covers your backend before you rely on it. See the warning under OpenAI Privacy Filter (Optional) above.
L239: Vulnerability Disclosure (Full Policy)
L240: 
L241: Reporting. Email security@entire.io. Do not open a public GitHub issue for a security vulnerability.Include in your report:
L242: 
L243:   * A clear description of the vulnerability.
L244:   * The impact, meaning what an attacker could achieve.
L245:   * Detailed steps to reproduce.
L246:   * Affected CLI versions if known.
L247:   * A suggested fix if you have one (optional).
L248: What to expect:
L249:   * Acknowledgment of receipt within 48 hours.
L250:   * Progress updates as we investigate.
L251:   * Resolution within 90 days for critical vulnerabilities.
L252: Confidentiality. We keep all reports confidential and will not share your information with third parties without your consent, except where the law requires it.Scope. The CLI (`entire`), official Entire GitHub repositories, and entire.com services.Out of scope (report upstream or treat as bug reports):
L253:   * Issues in third-party dependencies.
L254:   * Social engineering attacks.
L255:   * Denial of service that requires local access to trigger.
L256:   * Issues that cannot be exploited without direct access to the user’s machine.
L257: Bug reports vs security advisories. We reserve security advisories for confirmed vulnerabilities that a remote or non-local actor can exploit. Because the CLI is primarily a local development tool, we track regular-expression performance issues (ReDoS) on local execution, resource exhaustion that requires local access, and issues that cannot be exploited without direct machine access as bug reports. File those at 【29†github.com/entireio/cli/issues†github.com】.

L33: ## The Two Storage Backends
L34: 
L35: The backend controls how Git organizes checkpoint data. It is a separate question from which repository receives that data.
L36: ### Ref-Based Storage
L37: Ref-based storage (`git-refs`) is the default. It gives each new checkpoint its own Git ref, a named pointer inside your repository that Entire creates and manages for you. Each ref lives at `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>`, and Entire saves and retrieves each checkpoint independently. The benefit: With ref-based storage, pushes and reads stay fast even as your repository accumulates more agent history.
L38: Multiple agents can also save their work at the same time without competing to update a shared branch. Ref-based checkpoints use 26-character, time-sortable ULIDs, such as `01KVBJCWYA4YW6J5M9GP655HZN`. Ref-based storage first shipped as an opt-in option in Entire CLI 0.8.42 and became the default in 0.10.0, where `entire enable` writes it during a first-time setup and no longer asks you to choose.
L39: ### Branch-Based Storage
L40: Branch-based storage (`git-branch`) keeps every checkpoint on a shared Git branch called 【11†`entire/checkpoints/v1`】. Each checkpoint sits at `<first two characters of the ID>/<rest of the ID>/` in the branch tree. The benefit: All checkpoint history lives on one branch you can check out, browse, or clone like any other branch. Branch-based checkpoints use 12-character hexadecimal IDs, such as `a3b2c4d5e6f7`.
L41: A repository you enabled before Entire CLI 0.10.0 uses branch-based storage and stays on it until you 【12†switch backends】.
L42: ## Find Which Backend a Repository Uses
L43: 
L44: The backend is named by `checkpoints.primary.type` in `.entire/settings.json`, or in `.entire/settings.local.json` when someone set it for their clone alone. An absent `checkpoints` block resolves to `git-branch`, which is why a pre-0.10.0 repository keeps branch storage without any setting naming it. Checkpoint storage is ordinary Git, so Git reads it without Entire installed. List the per-checkpoint refs:
L45: 
L46:     `git for-each-ref refs/entire/checkpoints/
L47:     `
L48: Each line names one checkpoint, where `<shard>` is the last two characters of the ID and `<id>` is always the leaf. Check for branch-backed checkpoints too:
L49: 
L50:     `git show-ref entire/checkpoints/v1
L51:     `
L52: 
L53: Output from both means the repository holds checkpoints in both formats, which is the expected state after a backend switch. To confirm what reached the remote, run `git ls-remote origin 'refs/entire/checkpoints/*'`.
L54: ## Both Backends Stay Readable
L55: 
L56: Every reader routes by ID format, so one repository can hold both formats at once. This holds for the CLI, entire.com, and the Entire API.
L57: 
L58: Checkpoint ID  | Where the read goes
L59: --- | ---
L60: ULID  | Refs only. ULIDs are minted only under ref-based storage
L61: Hex, branch-based backend  | The `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch
L62: Hex, ref-based backend  | Refs first, then the branch, since a hex checkpoint may still sit on the pre-switch branch
L63: `entire checkpoint list` merges both backends and de-duplicates by ID. A new checkpoint goes to the configured backend, while a backfill that adds a transcript, summary, or attribution to an existing checkpoint lands in whichever backend already holds it.
L64: ## Switch Backends
L65: 
L66: To enable ref-based storage in a new repository, run:
L67: 
L68:     `entire enable --checkpoint-backend refs
L69:     `
L70: 
L71: To enable it in an existing Entire-enabled repository, run:
L72: 
L73:     `entire configure --checkpoint-backend refs
L74:     `
L75: Both commands accept `refs` and `branch`, plus the canonical `git-refs` and `git-branch` that settings store. Add `--local` when the choice should apply only to your clone. A switch applies to new checkpoints. Checkpoints written before the switch stay exactly where they are and keep resolving through the routing above, so `entire checkpoint list`, `entire checkpoint explain`, attribution, and entire.com continue to serve them.
L76: Entire deletes nothing during a switch, and your commands and commit workflow do not change. Two things do change after a switch to ref-based storage. New checkpoint IDs become ULIDs instead of hex, and the pre-push hook starts pushing queued per-checkpoint refs instead of the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch. Leave that branch on the remote: it is where readers find every checkpoint captured before the switch.
L77: ## Migrate Existing Checkpoints into Refs
L78: 
L79: Migration is optional, since the routing above already resolves branch-backed checkpoints under a ref-based backend. Migrate when you want the whole history in one format, or when you want to stop carrying the v1 branch.
L80: Run the migration before you switch the backend to refs. The command refuses to run once ref-based storage is primary, because the refs are authoritative at that point and re-importing branch snapshots could only move them backwards.
L81: 
L82:     `entire doctor migrate-checkpoints --dry-run
L83:     entire doctor migrate-checkpoints
L84:     `
L85: The command wraps each checkpoint’s current tree in a fresh commit and points its ref at it, keeping the hex ID as the ref name. It does not rewrite the branch commits, and it does not delete the branch. It skips checkpoints it has already converted, so you can re-run it after more branch activity.
L86: 
L87: Flag  | Description
L88: --- | ---
L89: `--dry-run`  | Report what would be migrated without writing refs
L90: `--remote NAME`  | Push migrated refs to this remote instead of the checkpoint sync remote
L91: Migrated refs are queued for push. Run interactively, the command asks whether to push them now. Run without a terminal, it leaves them queued, and they flush on the next `git push` once ref-based storage is primary. Then switch and push:
L92: 
L93:     `entire configure --checkpoint-backend refs
L94:     git push
L95:     `
L96: ## Auto-Generate Checkpoint Summaries
L97: 
L98: Checkpoint metadata can carry a summary generated at commit time. Enable it with `strategy_options.summarize.enabled`:
L99: 
L100: .entire/settings.json
L101: 
L102:     `{
L103:       "strategy_options": {
L104:         "summarize": {
L105:           "enabled": true
L106:         }
L107:       }
L108:     }
L109:     `
L110: 
L111: Then choose the provider and model:
L112: 
L113:     `entire configure --summarize-provider PROVIDER
L114:     entire configure --summarize-model MODEL
L115:     `
L116: Without a configured provider, commit-time summaries use Claude Code (`claude` on your `PATH`, model `sonnet`). `entire checkpoint explain --generate` instead picks an installed agent that can write summaries, asks when there are several, and saves your choice. Factory AI Droid cannot generate summaries.
L117: ## Where Storage Settings Are Saved
L118: `entire configure` writes to `.entire/settings.json` by default, so the repository shares the setting. Add `--local` to write `.entire/settings.local.json` instead, which applies only to your clone and takes precedence over project settings. The `checkpoints` block is a selection, not a merged document: a `checkpoints` block in `.entire/settings.local.json` replaces the one in `.entire/settings.json` outright.
L119: `strategy_options` merges only its top-level keys, so a nested object such as `summarize` or `checkpoint_remote` in the local file replaces the project one. See 【13†Local and Project Settings】 for the full table.

L130: When it runs. OPF runs at push time, not at commit time. Local commits stay on the eight regex layers, so per-commit latency is unchanged. During `git push`, the pre-push hook re-reads each unpushed checkpoint commit, runs the model over its content, and writes new commits carrying an `Entire-OPF-Applied: true` trailer. The local ref fast-forwards to the rewritten tip, and those commits are what reach the remote. The original commits become unreachable and are swept by `git gc`.Two consequences follow.

An image holding a credential, a customer record, or a screenshot of a dashboard reaches the remote intact, whether it sits inline in the transcript or in `assets/`.Externalization is off by default. Turning it on keeps large binary blobs out of the transcript files, which makes transcripts cheaper to read and diff. It does not add or remove any redaction coverage.

L71: `--transcript`  | Stream stored checkpoint transcript bytes (JSONL) to stdout: a session’s, or a subagent’s with `--task`
L74: `--json` emits metadata only. With no target it lists checkpoints; with a target it emits a single checkpoint envelope, including its subagent task records under `tasks` and the full session token breakdown (`subagent_tokens`, `subagent_tokens_complete`, `api_call_count`). Transcript bytes are never embedded in that envelope. To get the transcript itself, use `--transcript`, which streams the stored checkpoint transcript bytes to standard output:

L79:     entire checkpoint explain 01KVBJCW --transcript --task TOOL_USE_ID > subagent.jsonl
L83: `--repo` reads a checkpoint owned by a different repository through that repository’s Entire API. It takes a forge-qualified reference — `gh/OWNER/REPO` or `et/PROJECT/REPO`, or a full `entire://` URL — and refuses a bare `owner/repo`. This is the drill-down for a cross-repo 【11†`entire search`】 hit. Nothing is written to the current repository.
L85:     `entire checkpoint explain CHECKPOINT_ID --repo gh/owner/name
L87: This needs the full checkpoint ID, passed positionally or with `--checkpoint`, and a checkpoint that has been pushed.
L88: ## checkpoint tokens
L92:     `entire checkpoint tokens CHECKPOINT_ID [flags]
L98: `--compare ID`  | Compare against a baseline checkpoint ID
L100: `--json` and `--agent-brief` are mutually exclusive. The report resolves its target through the same path as `checkpoint explain`: an unambiguous checkpoint ID prefix, or a commit-ish carrying an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer. Metadata missing locally is fetched from the checkpoint remote.

L104:     entire checkpoint tokens 01KVBJCW --json
L106: ## checkpoint delete
L108: Delete one checkpoint from this repository and from every checkpoint remote that holds it.
L110:     `entire checkpoint delete CHECKPOINT_ID [flags]
L113: The full checkpoint ID is required; prefixes are not accepted. Deleting from a remote cannot be undone. Without `--force`, the command asks for confirmation and refuses when it cannot prompt.
L119: `--local-only`  | Delete only the local copy; leave every remote untouched
L120: `--remote REMOTE`  | Limit remote deletion to this remote; the local copy is still deleted. Repeatable. `checkpoint_remote` names the dedicated checkpoint remote
L121: Deleting a checkpoint is not a full purge. Other checkpoints from the same session are listed but not deleted, and each one carries the session’s full transcript, so the session stays visible on entire.com while any of them remain. On the legacy `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch, the checkpoint is removed from the branch tip only, and the branch’s history still contains it.
L122: On the `git-branch` backend, a local removal reaches the sync remote on the next `git push`, so `--local-only` (or a `--remote` selection that leaves that remote out) is refused while it holds a copy or cannot be reached. With `push_sessions` disabled the removal is not pushed, but re-enabling it later pushes it.
